title: What Is ISO/IEC 18013-7, and How Does It Bring the Mobile Driver’s License to Online Transactions?
summary: An mDL built only for in-person checks cannot power the digital services people use every day, ISO/IEC 18013-7 brings secure credential verification to the web.
body_markdown:
An mDL that only works when you hand your phone to a clerk cannot help you open a bank account online.[ISO/IEC 18013-5](https://www.iso.org/standard/69084.html?ref=blog.spruceid.com) was built for that in-person moment: you tap or scan, the reader talks directly to your device, and a person is usually standing there to supervise. Remote onboarding, age-gated services, and account creation all happen without that clerk, and the 2021 standard was never designed for them.[ISO/IEC 18013-7](https://www.iso.org/standard/82772.html?ref=blog.spruceid.com) fills that gap.


## What ISO/IEC 18013-7 adds to the mDL


ISO/IEC 18013-7 extends the mobile driver's license (mDL) standard to support online verification. While ISO/IEC 18013-5 defines how an mDL is presented in person (such as by tapping a phone or scanning a QR code) ISO/IEC 18013-7 defines how the same credential can be securely shared with a verifier over the internet. This makes it possible to use an mDL for remote interactions, such as proving your identity or age on a website, without being physically present.


The distinction matters for architects. 18013-5 assumes physical proximity and often a supervising operator. 18013-7 removes both. That single change is what makes online mDL presentation possible, and it is also what introduces the trust problems covered further down. This is the same shift written about in[Presenting Your Digital ID Online: How It Works](https://blog.spruceid.com/presenting-your-digital-id-online-how-it-works/) : the privacy and trust properties that work in person have to be re-established when no one is watching the transaction.


## The two presentation paths


ISO/IEC 18013-7 supports two ways for a website to request a mobile driver's license from a digital wallet. One uses[OpenID for Verifiable Presentations](https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0.html?ref=blog.spruceid.com) (OID4VP), an open protocol that lets a website send a request directly to a wallet. The other uses the[W3C Digital Credentials API](https://www.w3.org/TR/digital-credentials/?ref=blog.spruceid.com) , where the web browser acts as a trusted intermediary between the website and the wallet.


Although the two approaches work differently behind the scenes, they serve the same purpose: helping a website confirm that it is communicating with a trusted wallet and allowing the wallet to verify that the request came from the intended website before sharing any information. This gives organizations flexibility to support online mDL verification across different browsers and devices.


The[W3C Digital Credentials API](https://www.w3.org/TR/digital-credentials/?ref=blog.spruceid.com) , a W3C Working Draft as of mid-2026, is the browser-native path. It lets a website request a credential such as a driver’s license, keeps interactions user-mediated behind a transient user gesture, and is designed to be agnostic to credential format. It can carry both OID4VP requests and the ISO mdoc protocol identifier, which is why the two paths in 18013-7 are complementary rather than competing.


## The same signed mdoc, reused online


ISO/IEC 18013-7 does not introduce a new type of mobile driver's license. Instead, it allows the same mDL a person already has on their phone to be used for online verification. Whether someone presents their credential in person or over the internet, the wallet uses the same issuer-signed credential and shares only the information needed for the transaction. In other words, the standard extends where an mDL can be used without changing the credential itself.


That reuse is what makes the system interoperable. States do not need to issue separate credentials for in-person and online use. The same mobile driver's license can be used in both settings, making it easier for agencies and relying parties to support a single, standards-based credential across many services. This is the core idea behind[What Is Interoperability in Government Digital Services? (And Why It's Not Optional)](https://blog.spruceid.com/interoperability-what-is-interoperability-in-government-digital-services-and-why-its-not-optional/) : one credential that works across many contexts, rather than separate solutions for each use case.


## The hard part: verifier impersonation and phishing


Remote credential presentation invites an attack that the in-person flow mostly prevents through physical proximity. When no operator supervises the exchange, an attacker can set up a fake verifier, lure a holder into presenting, and relay the identity data to a real service. 18013-7 addresses this with two mechanisms.


The first is mdoc reader authentication, inherited from ISO/IEC 18013-5. An mDL can require the reader to authenticate before releasing any mandatory data element, which in turn requires a pre-existing trust relationship, typically expressed through X.509 certificates. The second is origin binding, which matters specifically for the browser path. For Digital Credentials API retrieval, the user agent passes the caller’s web origin to the mdoc; the mdoc and the reader both include that origin in the session transcript, so the origin has to match on both sides. A relayed request from a phishing site carries the wrong origin and fails. These are the online equivalents of the trust properties we describe in the context of[offline-capable verifiable digital credentials](https://blog.spruceid.com/digitalidentity-what-does-offline-capable-mean-when-it-comes-to-verifiable-digital-credentials/) , where verification integrity cannot depend on a live connection to the issuer.


## What states should require before turning on online acceptance


Online acceptance is a policy decision as much as a technical one. Before enabling it, an issuing authority should confirm four things:


1. **Trusted verifier ecosystem.** Wallets need a reliable way to confirm that a request is coming from an approved verifier before sharing any information.
2. **Protection against phishing.** Online presentations should be tied to the website requesting the credential, so users do not accidentally share information with an impersonator.
3. **Selective disclosure by default.** Verifiers should request only the information they need, such as confirming that someone is over 21 rather than collecting a full driver's license.
4. **Support for current standards.** Because digital identity standards continue to evolve, wallets and verifiers should implement compatible, up-to-date versions.


ISO/IEC 18013-7 extends a proven in-person credential to the web without forcing states to reissue anything. The engineering that makes it safe, verifier trust and origin binding, is the part worth getting right before the first online transaction.
